Since the exhibit page's intro already functions as a mini write-up (the landing five demonstrate this), I'm leaning toward having the exhibit page carry the full public argument.

The digest email becomes its own artifact — a letter-style version with "when to reach for it" framing plus banked reveals, so there's no conflict between the two and no need for a public digest archive right now. That resolves cleanly enough to mention in one paragraph.

Now I'm thinking about how to write the final message — matching Eric's register as a developer-educator who appreciates craft, following the repo's convention of options plus recommendation plus trade-offs, keeping the prose alive without performing. I shouldn't imitate voice.md's style for my own message since that's meant for site copy, but I also don't want to sound bureaucratic. I'll structure it with a few headers, lead with the outcome, and end with the right close.

I want to directly address Eric's Mintlify comparison — sharpening the point that docs organize reference material for lookup, while the playground organizes arguments in sequence for a gallery-like experience, and crucially its pages must execute rather than just describe. That's the real cash-out of "more than a doc site": Mintlify embeds interactive widgets that simulate, but here the page itself is the feature. I also confirm the URL segment stays in English across locales, which is standard and fine.

So "at least eight of seventeen" is the safer, defensible number. I'm also weighing whether route-shaped demos could technically live as sub-routes without a full per-exhibit page shell, hanging off the landing sections instead.

That alternative would split the exhibit across a landing section and separate demo routes, hurting shareability and bloating the landing page further — so I'll fold that rejection into my main argument rather than treating it separately. I'm trimming the "shells considered" comparison down to short prose paragraphs rather than a table, and sketching the final message structure: a TLDR on the overall shape, followed by a compact grounding paragraph covering what I found, including the syllabus locations, the orphaned blog, untouched Mintlify setup, and the digest model.

content.text:
The explorer's report landed and it settles several open questions — the syllabus lives in three places (the `UPCOMING` array, the masterclass specs, the digest DB model), the blog machinery is wired but orphaned, and `apps/docs` (Mintlify) is untouched boilerplate with zero project content. I have everything needed to shape the proposal. Here it is — this is a design round, so I'm presenting the shape and stopping for your yes before anything gets built.

---

## The recommendation in two sentences

Give the collection the shape of a **numbered, serialized web book whose chapters are running instruments**: one flat contents page at `/exhibits`, one route segment per exhibit at `/exhibits/<slug>`, all driven by a single syllabus registry — not a Mintlify-style doc site, and not the landing page growing forever. The deciding fact isn't taste: **at least eight of the seventeen upcoming topics are made of routes** — parallel & intercepted routes, error/not-found, dynamic params, redirects, view transitions, i18n, ISR, navigation itself — so they physically cannot live on any single page; each exhibit must own a route segment, and the only open question was ever the shell around those segments.

## What grounds this

I read the landing page, `voice.md`, `design.md`, and had the repo swept. Things that shaped the proposal: the syllabus already exists in code (`UPCOMING`, 17 topics, plus 5 shipped exhibits — 22 chapters total); the site's words are already book-and-museum words (`chapter="01"`, "exhibits", a nav literally labeled "contents"); the digest has a real data model in MongoDB with a `misconception` field and a `series/part` structure, authored in `apps/app`; a local-MDX blog route is fully wired but linked from nowhere; `apps/docs` is dead Mintlify boilerplate ("Starter Kit", plant-store API); and the masterclass lives separately under `/learn/…`. Also: the contents nav, the `UPCOMING` list, and the per-demo `chapter` props are three hand-maintained copies of the same knowledge.

## Why not the two obvious shells

**The doc site (Mintlify shape — sidebar tree, categories, search).** Docs organize *reference*: you arrive knowing what to look up, and the sidebar is a filing cabinet. This collection organizes *arguments* — every exhibit is a rebuttal to a belief, sequenced by a teacher — and `design.md` is explicit that the feel is "a developer environment, not a course platform." A persistent sidebar is course-platform chrome, and it frames each page as *a page about* streaming. The whole identity of this site is that the page *is* the streaming. Interactivity in doc sites means embedded widgets simulating the feature; here the claim "nothing on this page is a mockup" has to hold on every surface. (Also: there's no sunk investment pulling this way — `apps/docs` is empty boilerplate.)

**The single growing page (the current trajectory).** Dies twice: at 22 exhibits the page's weight and the contents bar both collapse, and the route-shaped exhibits can't board at all. The nearest variant — keep landing sections but hang auxiliary demo routes off them — splits each exhibit's home from its body and ruins per-exhibit shareability.

**The book (recommended).** The spine register of the site is already Matthew Butterick, and *Practical Typography* is the existing artifact closest to what this should feel like: a self-published web book, spare chrome, a table of contents and chapters, the artifact itself demonstrating its subject. This is that, except the chapters run. The Monday cadence makes it a *serialized* book — chapters ship weekly, the bound volume accretes, numbers are accession order. (If the wall ever gets crowded, thematic shelving can come later — the number stays, the shelf can move. Not now; 22 rows fit on one screen.)

## The design

**One registry.** A `syllabus.ts` in the web app — number, slug, topic, belief, status, shipped date per exhibit — replacing the three hand-maintained lists. It drives the contents page, the landing roadmap, the contents nav, prev/next links, the sitemap, and each page's metadata. Shipping an exhibit becomes: merge the folder, flip the registry entry.

**The contents page, `/exhibits` — a floor plan with the lights on.** The syllabus made navigable: shipped chapters as rows (number, belief as the link text — an index of things you were sure about — topic eyebrow), upcoming ones as the `+` rows the roadmap already renders, the next Monday marked. The distinctive move no doc sidebar can make: where it's cheap and true, a row carries **one live value from the running exhibit** — the cache row wears the current bake fingerprint, the mutation row the press count — each row Suspense-streamed, so the index itself is an instrument panel and, incidentally, a PPR demonstration. Digest capture at the bottom; this page's visitors are the most convertible ones.

**The exhibit page — the chapter anatomy, scaled up from `DemoSection`.** Belief as the H1, the intro escort at full length, the instrument(s) in the fixed chassis, the aside, the reference bar — plus what only a dedicated page affords: child routes when the topic *is* routes (the address bar joins the instrument — the masterclass's `address-strip.tsx` already prototyped this), a **making-of strip** linking the PR and the checkpoint transcript (no docs site on earth has this), prev/next by number, and its own OG card drawn by the existing `/api/og` with the belief as the title — which quietly makes exhibit 05's central claim, "one file draws the card for every page you will ever publish," literally true across the whole collection. The exhibit page's prose is the write-up's permanent public home; the Monday email stays the letter version with the banked reveals (`design.md` §5 banks them for exactly this).

**The landing page's new job: front door, not the whole building.** Nothing moves. The five built exhibits stay inline — they're the best sales material the site has — but their demo wrappers get extracted from `page.tsx` so each also renders at its own `/exhibits/<slug>`, giving every chapter a canonical URL from day one (a senior can drop `/exhibits/caching` into a code review instead of explaining; that's the shareability requirement cashed out). The roadmap section becomes a live excerpt of the contents page. One copy line needs re-anchoring per `voice.md` §7: "A new demo lands on this page" is about to stop being true — it becomes a structural truth about the site, not the page.

**Monday, structurally.** Merge exhibit folder, flip registry entry, email links the exhibit URL, a stable `/latest` redirect always points at the newest chapter (and is itself redirect-exhibit material). First chapter on the new shape writes its own narrative beat: **exhibit 06, navigation & prefetching, whose specimen is the playground's own contents page** — the exhibit that explains why the site became multi-page, demonstrated by the pages it became.

**The doctrine that keeps it from becoming a doc site:** wherever possible, the collection's own chrome is built from the syllabus. The 404 page is the not-found exhibit. The vitals exhibit measures this site's real field data. The i18n exhibit is the `[locale]` segment everything already sits in. The flags exhibit flips something visible site-wide. View transitions arrive between exhibit pages the week that chapter ships. The playground grows by eating its own features — which is also the honest version of "interactive."

## What it deliberately isn't

No embedded sandbox or editable REPL — a sandbox runs a *copy*, and the site's entire authority is that you're poking the production feature itself; hands-on is the cohort's job and the public repo's. No search until the contents page outgrows a screen. No per-level modes. No new CMS — exhibits are code, and code-as-content is the product.

## Named trade-offs

More upfront structure than stacking the landing page (registry, contents page, five thin pages, one extraction refactor) — amortized by every Monday after. Per-page metadata/a11y/OG polish becomes a repeated cost — the registry and shared chassis absorb most of it. Live contents rows add server work to the index — bounded by using only values that are already cached or one cookie read, and rows degrade to plain.

**Housekeeping the sweep surfaced** (separate, whenever): `apps/docs` is deletable dead weight, `(counter)/` is orphaned, `/pricing` is off-voice next-forge boilerplate, and the wired-but-unlinked blog could later serve as the digest archive (the `series/part` model already anticipates one).

---

**Your call.** Does the book shape get a yes? Three decisions inside it I'd like your explicit word on: **(1)** the URL word — I recommend `/exhibits` over `/playground`, `/demos`, `/x`; **(2)** the five landing exhibits also getting their own canonical pages via extraction — recommended, since a collection whose first five chapters are anchor links undercuts the grammar; **(3)** live values on contents rows — recommended, it's the single most "this could only be hasToggle" element of the index. Nothing gets built until you say so.

# The lab — approved design (2026-08-20)

Status: **approved by Eric** (companion session, 2026-08-20 evening). Untracked
by convention; this file is the build contract for whichever workspace
implements it.

Approvals on record: book shape ✓ · canonical pages for the five built
exhibits ✓ · live values on contents rows ✓ · URL word `/lab` ✓ ("lab is
perfect"). Rejected shells: doc-site (sidebar/reference posture), single
growing page. Rejected URL words: /exhibits (museum vocabulary), /poke
(spends the brand verb on chrome), /proof (overclaims before the panel
loads), /press, /bench, /run, /live, /on, /toggles, /beliefs (labels the
confrontation — voice.md §4).

## Shape

A serialized web book whose chapters run. One flat contents page at
`/[locale]/lab`, one route segment per exhibit at `/[locale]/lab/<slug>`,
everything driven by a single syllabus registry. Forcing fact: at least 8 of
the 17 upcoming topics are made of routes (parallel/intercepted, error/
not-found, dynamic params, redirects, view transitions, i18n, ISR,
navigation) and cannot live on any single page. Feel: Practical Typography
whose chapters execute — spare chrome, numbered chapters, prev/next, no
sidebar. The word "lab" is rooted in shipped copy: "the lab bench that
belongs next to them" (FAQ). Naming principle: the address names a place
(noun); "poking" stays the verb on the pages.

## Registry — `syllabus.ts` (apps/web)

One entry per chapter; single source of truth replacing three hand lists
(UPCOMING, ContentsNav CHAPTERS, DemoSection chapter props).

- `n` ("01"…), `slug`, `topic` (eyebrow text), `navLabel` ("The cache"),
  `belief` (present once shipped), `status: shipped | next | planned`,
  `shippedOn`.
- Drives: /lab rows + upcoming `+` list, landing Roadmap excerpt,
  ContentsNav, prev/next, sitemap entries, per-page metadata + OG title,
  `/latest` target (highest shipped `n`).

Slugs for the five (defaults, changeable in review): `boundary`, `caching`,
`streaming`, `server-actions`, `og-images`. Chapter 06 (next): `navigation`
(navigation & prefetching). Slugs are short, topical, stable forever —
internal folder names (shell, stream, mutation…) stay as they are.

## Contents page — `/lab`

- Shipped rows: number · belief (the link text) · topic eyebrow · one live
  value. `next` row marked (lands Monday, amber dot). Remaining topics as
  the `+` rows the landing roadmap already renders. Digest capture at the
  bottom.
- Live values, bounded: a shipped exhibit MAY export a small server
  component (`IndexValue`) from its folder; the row renders it inside
  Suspense; absent → plain row. Truth rule: the value must be literally
  true — 04's cookie count is per-visitor, so it reads as *your* presses,
  never a global count. 01: node version · 02: bake fingerprint + swatch
  (cached, shares the landing tag) · 03: static delay label · 05: static
  `1200 × 630 · png`.
- The index streams its rows — it is itself a PPR demonstration.
- Banked for chapter 06: hover-prefetch readout in the contents rows (the
  navigation exhibit's instrument living in the site chrome).

## Chapter page — `/lab/<slug>`

DemoSection grammar scaled to a page: belief as H1, topic eyebrow
(`02 · caching & revalidation`), intro at full walkthrough length (landing
intro is the trailer), the instrument chassis unchanged, the aside, the
reference bar. Plus what only a page affords:

- **Child routes** when the topic is routes — the exhibit owns its segment
  (error.tsx, [param], @slots, interceptors live inside it); the browser
  address bar joins the instrument.
- **Making-of strip**: PR · checkpoint transcript · prompts (links per
  exhibit; checkpoints repo already public).
- **Prev/next** by number, using `navLabel`.
- **Metadata/OG**: title from the belief; OG card drawn by the existing
  `/api/og?title=` — exhibit 05's "one file draws the card for every page"
  becomes literally true.
- The chapter page is the write-up's permanent public home; the Monday
  email stays the letter edition (banked reveals in design.md §5 are its
  exclusives).

## Landing page changes

- Extract the five wrapper functions (BoundaryDemo, ShellDemo, StreamDemo,
  MutationDemo, ImageDemo) from `page.tsx` into their `(playground)`
  folders; landing renders them unchanged (pixel-identical), chapter pages
  import the same wrappers. Shared instrument state across pages (the bake
  tag, the press cookie) is intended — "one entry, shared by every visitor"
  stays true.
- Roadmap section becomes a registry-driven excerpt linking to /lab.
- ContentsNav derives from the registry; gains a trailing link into /lab.
- Copy re-anchor (voice.md §7): DigestCTA's "A new demo lands on this
  page." stops being true when 06 ships elsewhere — rewrite via voice
  passes, structural phrasing.
- `/latest`: standing redirect to the newest shipped chapter (later:
  redirects-exhibit material).

## Monday runbook

merge exhibit folder → flip registry entry (planned → shipped, belief in) →
contents row lights up / roadmap shrinks / sitemap + OG appear (all
derived) → digest email links `/lab/<slug>` → `/latest` follows.

## Non-goals

No sandbox/REPL (a sandbox runs a copy; the site's authority is the real
thing running). No search until the contents page outgrows a screen. No
per-level modes. No new CMS — exhibits are code.

## Deferred / adjacent (not in scope)

- Prose vocabulary: "exhibit" stays in shipped copy for now; museum→lab
  migration is a separate copy decision taken with voice.md open.
- Digest public archive (DB model already has series/part/misconception);
  the wired-but-orphaned /blog could host it later.
- Housekeeping: apps/docs is dead Mintlify boilerplate; `(counter)/` is
  orphaned; /pricing is off-voice next-forge boilerplate.

## Build order (slices, each independently verifiable)

1. `syllabus.ts` + tests; ContentsNav, Roadmap, chapter props derive from
   it — landing visually unchanged.
2. Extract the five demo wrappers — landing pixel-identical, tests pass.
3. `/lab` contents page (plain rows) + sitemap + metadata + digest capture;
   its headline copy goes through voice.md's three passes with Eric.
4. Five chapter pages (wrapper + prose + making-of + prev/next + OG).
5. Live index values (Suspense) + `/latest` redirect. Cache-touching
   values verified on a preview deploy (design.md §6: dev lies).
6. Landing copy re-anchors (voice passes).

Verification: every slice ends with Biome + typecheck + the web app's
tests green, and anything touching `use cache` proven on a preview deploy,
not `next dev`.

content.thinking:
With slice 2 pushed, I'm now planning slice 3: five chapter pages under /lab/[slug]. I'm weighing static folders per slug versus a dynamic route, leaning toward static folders like lab/boundary/page.tsx and lab/caching/page.tsx since the exhibits differ enough (some need searchParams, others may need child routes) that dedicated tiny pages make more sense than one generic dynamic handler.

I'm sketching a shared ChapterPage frame that wraps navbar, demo wrapper, making-of section, prev/next nav, and footer — but I realize DemoSection already renders the eyebrow and belief heading, so I need to check what heading level it uses in demo-section.tsx to make sure it's semantically correct as an h1 on a standalone chapter page.

I'm also weighing whether the layout should include scroll-driven reveal animations like the landing page does, but since chapter content sits at the top of the viewport those reveals would likely fire immediately anyway — I'll leave it as-is and verify visually. Now I'm thinking through how the making-of strip should link out per exhibit.

Real per-exhibit PR numbers don't exist cleanly — exhibits were built across many PRs, so fabricating specific links would violate the truth rule. I'm leaning toward a more honest, generic approach: link to the repo folder, the checkpoints repo root, and this PR itself, rather than inventing precise per-exhibit provenance, though that risks duplicating the reference bar's existing source link.

That gives me the strip format: making-of, every commit, prompts & checkpoints. Since the registry doesn't track folder paths, I'll just have each chapter page pass its own commitsHref and related links directly to the shared frame component rather than centralizing it.

For prev/next navigation, I'll derive it from the registry's prevNext(slug) helper, using the navLabel as-is in the mono strip rather than inventing a lowercase transform, and handling the edge cases where 01 has no prev or 05 links back to the lab contents. I'm settling on "The lab" as the eyebrow, "Contents." as the heading, and a standfirst that swaps "exhibit" for "chapter" so the new page doesn't borrow the museum metaphor from the landing copy. Now I'm working out the layout for the shipped-chapters list — each row as a link with a number, title, and topic label arranged in a grid.

For typography I'm using a muted mono number, a larger display-weight title, and a small mono topic tag, with the same underline-draw hover effect reused from ContentsNav. I'm leaving room in the grid for a future live-value slot, and for the upcoming unshipped row I'm deciding against an amber dot (too easily confused with the in-progress gauge) in favor of plain mono text noting it "lands Monday."

For the planned items I'm reusing the same two-column "+" list markup from the landing roadmap, and at the bottom I'm sketching a compact digest capture block — a bordered divider with a small "The weekly build" subheading and a short line about the Monday cadence, scaled down from the landing page's larger CTA section.

I like "what's running, what lands Monday, what's still to build" as a true description of the page's three list states. For the OG title I need to check what the default title convention is before deciding between something like "The lab: contents" or just "Contents" — I should peek at the title helper to see what's already established. I'm also wondering whether the contents page needs a nav link alongside the chapter shell's plain logo.

Now I'm thinking about how to get back to /lab from chapter pages — the navbar's links array is currently empty, and I could add a "The lab" entry there, but that would affect every page's top-right nav, not just chapters. Since the burger menu was removed earlier because there was nowhere for it to lead, and now there's finally a destination, adding this link feels like it could be the right move, though I want to weigh whether it's in scope for this change.

Everything checks out — the contents page renders correctly with all rows and links, and the sitemap confirms all 6 lab entries. I'll commit this slice and push, then move to slice 5: building live index values and the /latest route, starting with an IndexValue component for the boundary exhibit that prints the Node.js version from a server component.

For the shell exhibit, I'll reuse the existing BakeSwatch component to render the cached bake data with its swatch and id. The stream exhibit needs actual delay constants from rows.ts, the mutation exhibit reads a press-count cookie dynamically (so it must live inside Suspense), and the image exhibit is just a static dimension label. Now I'm figuring out where these live values actually slot into the existing row grid layout, since the mockup placed them on the right but the current grid structure doesn't obviously accommodate that.

I'm redesigning the row so the topic always sits on a second line under the belief text, freeing up the third grid column for the right-aligned live value, which I'll hide on mobile and show only at sm breakpoints and up, with an empty aria-hidden span as the Suspense fallback to keep layout stable.

Now I'm realizing there's a routing problem: /latest is a top-level route handler outside the locale structure, but it isn't in the i18n middleware's exclusion list, so the middleware would try to rewrite it to /en/latest, which doesn't exist and would 404.

The fix is to move the route handler under the [locale] segment so /latest correctly rewrites to /en/latest and resolves, then have it redirect to the canonical unprefixed /lab/<slug> path using the LATEST syllabus entry — redirect() from next/navigation works fine in route handlers and returns a 307, so I don't need NextResponse.redirect with an absolute URL.

No new cache surface risk since there are no new tags, so a preview smoke check should suffice — fetching both /lab and / on the preview deploy and comparing their fingerprints proves the shared tag works. toolUseResult.originalFile:
# The instrument design guide

`voice.md`'s sibling: that guide governs what a visitor reads, this one
governs what they see and press. It exists for the same reason — the design
drifts, and it drifts toward decoration. Every element on a demo earns its
place by answering one question: does this contribute to clarity? The page's
feel is a developer environment, not a course platform. Engineer, not
student.

The audience is four people at once — an aspiring developer, a non-technical
visitor, a junior, a senior — and they get **one experience legible at all
levels, never per-level modes**. When a value needs to reach all four, encode
it redundantly (two channels, one display), don't fork the interface.

---

## 1. The fixed grammar

Every demo sits in the same chassis, zones in fixed positions — like a car's
cockpit or an editor's panes, a visitor who has used one instrument has used
them all:

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ ● live                        SLOW MOTION ⭘ │  chrome: state left, view right
│                                              │
│  bake #64f93b                                │  the specimen
│  provenance rows · one narration caption     │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ [ actions, in execution order ]              │  the deck
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ ▸ bake.ts + actions.ts       docs ↗ source ↗ │  reference bar
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

- **Chrome, top-left — the state gauge.** `live` (cyan) at rest, `working`
  (amber) while any server round trip is out. One in-flight signal per
  instrument; this is it.
- **Chrome, top-right — view controls.** Mode switches (slow motion) live in
  the corner every editor keeps its view switches. Actions never live here.
  Empty when a demo has no alternate view.
- **Body — the specimen.** The observed value large, provenance rows as one
  aligned table, one narration caption. All describing text in one place.
- **Deck — actions only.** Execution order, left to right. When a flow has
  real sequence, the controls diagram it (numbered steps, an arrow, the later
  step dark until the earlier one fires). A deck may end in a **result chip —
  output, never input** — when the platform's own label for the sequence's
  outcome is knowable by rule (exhibit 02: `revalidated · tag-based
  deletion`, the badge Vercel files the refill under).
- **Reference bar — the status bar every editor ends in.** The code drawer's
  disclosure left (source opens inside the chassis, native `<details>`, zero
  JS); `docs` and `source` links pinned right, positioned so clicking them
  never toggles the drawer. Row height mirrors the chrome header.

What the grammar deliberately lacks: a panel label (the intro prose names the
subject once) and a readout footer (the source in the drawer is the spec
plate — a reader who wants identifiers is the reader who opens it).

Outside the chassis: exhibit order rides in the eyebrow (`02 · caching &
revalidation`) where engineers read identifiers — no watermark chapter
numerals. Asides are set as `/* code comments */` in comment-gray mono,
because that is what they are.

## 2. Feedback

Anything in flight says so three ways: the gauge flips to `working`, the
specimen dims and pulses, and when the new value lands it takes one amber
wash (`.ht-land` — key-remount, skips first paint, reduced-motion safe) and
settles. No silent updates, ever.

The React rule underneath: **client-owned state paints on the click frame;
only the server sync lives in a transition.** A mode flip inside the same
transition as its `router.refresh()` freezes the control until the round
trip resolves. While the flipped view waits for the server, the copy must
narrate the in-flight window honestly rather than claim a state the screen
doesn't show (see the settling readout in `rebake-copy.ts`).

## 3. Copy and demo co-evolve

A demo that gains a capability can obsolete prose that was accurate the day

# The instrument design guide

`voice.md`'s sibling: that guide governs what a visitor reads, this one
governs what they see and press. It exists for the same reason — the design
drifts, and it drifts toward decoration. Every element on a demo earns its
place by answering one question: does this contribute to clarity? The page's
feel is a developer environment, not a course platform. Engineer, not
student.

The audience is four people at once — an aspiring developer, a non-technical
visitor, a junior, a senior — and they get **one experience legible at all
levels, never per-level modes**. When a value needs to reach all four, encode
it redundantly (two channels, one display), don't fork the interface.

---

## 1. The fixed grammar

Every demo sits in the same chassis, zones in fixed positions — like a car's
cockpit or an editor's panes, a visitor who has used one instrument has used
them all:

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ ● live                        SLOW MOTION ⭘ │  chrome: state left, view right
│                                              │
│  bake #64f93b                                │  the specimen
│  provenance rows · one narration caption     │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ [ actions, in execution order ]              │  the deck
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ ▸ bake.ts + actions.ts       docs ↗ source ↗ │  reference bar
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

- **Chrome, top-left — the state gauge.** `live` (cyan) at rest, `working`
  (amber) while any server round trip is out. One in-flight signal per
  instrument; this is it.
- **Chrome, top-right — view controls.** Mode switches (slow motion) live in
  the corner every editor keeps its view switches. Actions never live here.
  Empty when a demo has no alternate view.
- **Body — the specimen.** The observed value large, provenance rows as one
  aligned table, one narration caption. All describing text in one place.
- **Deck — actions only.** Execution order, left to right. When a flow has
  real sequence, the controls diagram it (numbered steps, an arrow, the later
  step dark until the earlier one fires). A deck may end in a **result chip —
  output, never input** — when the platform's own label for the sequence's
  outcome is knowable by rule (exhibit 02: `revalidated · tag-based
  deletion`, the badge Vercel files the refill under).
- **Reference bar — the status bar every editor ends in.** The code drawer's
  disclosure left (source opens inside the chassis, native `<details>`, zero
  JS); `docs` and `source` links pinned right, positioned so clicking them
  never toggles the drawer. Row height mirrors the chrome header.

What the grammar deliberately lacks: a panel label (the intro prose names the
subject once) and a readout footer (the source in the drawer is the spec
plate — a reader who wants identifiers is the reader who opens it).

Outside the chassis: exhibit order rides in the eyebrow (`02 · caching &
revalidation`) where engineers read identifiers — no watermark chapter
numerals. Asides are set as `/* code comments */` in comment-gray mono,
because that is what they are.

## 2. Feedback

Anything in flight says so three ways: the gauge flips to `working`, the
specimen dims and pulses, and when the new value lands it takes one amber
wash (`.ht-land` — key-remount, skips first paint, reduced-motion safe) and
settles. No silent updates, ever.

The React rule underneath: **client-owned state paints on the click frame;
only the server sync lives in a transition.** A mode flip inside the same
transition as its `router.refresh()` freezes the control until the round
trip resolves. While the flipped view waits for the server, the copy must
narrate the in-flight window honestly rather than claim a state the screen
doesn't show (see the settling readout in `rebake-copy.ts`).

# The lab — approved design (2026-08-20)

Status: **approved by Eric** (companion session, 2026-08-20 evening). Untracked
by convention; this file is the build contract for whichever workspace
implements it.

Approvals on record: book shape ✓ · canonical pages for the five built
exhibits ✓ · live values on contents rows ✓ · URL word `/lab` ✓ ("lab is
perfect"). Rejected shells: doc-site (sidebar/reference posture), single
growing page. Rejected URL words: /exhibits (museum vocabulary), /poke
(spends the brand verb on chrome), /proof (overclaims before the panel
loads), /press, /bench, /run, /live, /on, /toggles, /beliefs (labels the
confrontation — voice.md §4).

## Shape

A serialized web book whose chapters run. One flat contents page at
`/[locale]/lab`, one route segment per exhibit at `/[locale]/lab/<slug>`,
everything driven by a single syllabus registry. Forcing fact: at least 8 of
the 17 upcoming topics are made of routes (parallel/intercepted, error/
not-found, dynamic params, redirects, view transitions, i18n, ISR,
navigation) and cannot live on any single page. Feel: Practical Typography
whose chapters execute — spare chrome, numbered chapters, prev/next, no
sidebar. The word "lab" is rooted in shipped copy: "the lab bench that
belongs next to them" (FAQ). Naming principle: the address names a place
(noun); "poking" stays the verb on the pages.

## Registry — `syllabus.ts` (apps/web)

One entry per chapter; single source of truth replacing three hand lists
(UPCOMING, ContentsNav CHAPTERS, DemoSection chapter props).

- `n` ("01"…), `slug`, `topic` (eyebrow text), `navLabel` ("The cache"),
  `belief` (present once shipped), `status: shipped | next | planned`,
  `shippedOn`.
- Drives: /lab rows + upcoming `+` list, landing Roadmap excerpt,
  ContentsNav, prev/next, sitemap entries, per-page metadata + OG title,
  `/latest` target (highest shipped `n`).

Slugs for the five (defaults, changeable in review): `boundary`, `caching`,
`streaming`, `server-actions`, `og-images`. Chapter 06 (next): `navigation`
(navigation & prefetching). Slugs are short, topical, stable forever —
internal folder names (shell, stream, mutation…) stay as they are.

## Contents page — `/lab`

- Shipped rows: number · belief (the link text) · topic eyebrow · one live
  value. `next` row marked (lands Monday, amber dot). Remaining topics as
  the `+` rows the landing roadmap already renders. Digest capture at the
  bottom.
- Live values, bounded: a shipped exhibit MAY export a small server
  component (`IndexValue`) from its folder; the row renders it inside
  Suspense; absent → plain row. Truth rule: the value must be literally
  true — 04's cookie count is per-visitor, so it reads as *your* presses,
  never a global count. 01: node version · 02: bake fingerprint + swatch
  (cached, shares the landing tag) · 03: static delay label · 05: static
  `1200 × 630 · png`.
- The index streams its rows — it is itself a PPR demonstration.
- Banked for chapter 06: hover-prefetch readout in the contents rows (the
  navigation exhibit's instrument living in the site chrome).

## Chapter page — `/lab/<slug>`

DemoSection grammar scaled to a page: belief as H1, topic eyebrow
(`02 · caching & revalidation`), intro at full walkthrough length (landing
intro is the trailer), the instrument chassis unchanged, the aside, the
reference bar. Plus what only a page affords:

- **Child routes** when the topic is routes — the exhibit owns its segment
  (error.tsx, [param], @slots, interceptors live inside it); the browser
  address bar joins the instrument.
- **Making-of strip**: PR · checkpoint transcript · prompts (links per
  exhibit; checkpoints repo already public).
- **Prev/next** by number, using `navLabel`.
- **Metadata/OG**: title from the belief; OG card drawn by the existing
  `/api/og?title=` — exhibit 05's "one file draws the card for every page"
  becomes literally true.
- The chapter page is the write-up's permanent public home; the Monday
  email stays the letter edition (banked reveals in design.md §5 are its
  exclusives).

## Landing page changes

- Extract the five wrapper functions (BoundaryDemo, ShellDemo, StreamDemo,
  MutationDemo, ImageDemo) from `page.tsx` into their `(playground)`
  folders; landing renders them unchanged (pixel-identical), chapter pages
  import the same wrappers. Shared instrument state across pages (the bake

  redirects-exhibit material).

merge exhibit folder → flip registry entry (planned → shipped, belief in) →
contents row lights up / roadmap shrinks / sitemap + OG appear (all
derived) → digest email links `/lab/<slug>` → `/latest` follows.

No sandbox/REPL (a sandbox runs a copy; the site's authority is the real
thing running). No search until the contents page outgrows a screen. No
per-level modes. No new CMS — exhibits are code.

- Prose vocabulary: "exhibit" stays in shipped copy for now; museum→lab
  migration is a separate copy decision taken with voice.md open.
- Digest public archive (DB model already has series/part/misconception);
  the wired-but-orphaned /blog could host it later.
- Housekeeping: apps/docs is dead Mintlify boilerplate; `(counter)/` is
  orphaned; /pricing is off-voice next-forge boilerplate.

1. `syllabus.ts` + tests; ContentsNav, Roadmap, chapter props derive from
   it — landing visually unchanged.

3. `/lab` contents page (plain rows) + sitemap + metadata + digest capture;
   its headline copy goes through voice.md's three passes with Eric.
4. Five chapter pages (wrapper + prose + making-of + prev/next + OG).
5. Live index values (Suspense) + `/latest` redirect. Cache-touching
   values verified on a preview deploy (design.md §6: dev lies).
6. Landing copy re-anchors (voice passes).

tests green, and anything touching `use cache` proven on a preview deploy,
not `next dev`.

My broader swatch search was picking up unrelated inline colors, but filtering down I found the real bake swatches differ: landing shows #160305 while the lab row shows #caf7da. I'm now checking whether this is a genuine mismatch by looking at how getBake() uses cache tagging.

Since landing and /lab are separately prerendered pages, it's possible each invoked getBake() in a different build worker, producing two distinct baked values frozen into separate static shells — which would explain the discrepancy if the build cache wasn't shared across those renders. At runtime, pressing rebake deletes the tag and should revalidate the cached component on next request, and I know the landing flow works, so I'm now trying to figure out why /lab's row might be holding its own separate copy of the entry.

On Vercel though, since `use cache` entries live in the shared data cache separate from the ISR shell layer, both pages would eventually converge to the same fingerprint once both shells revalidate and hit that shared entry — but immediately post-build they'd still show whatever each isolated build worker baked, since parallel build workers likely don't share a single cache fill.

The claim in my index-value comment — that rebaking either page changes the row for everyone — holds true for the rebake flow itself, since tag deletion nukes the shared entry and both pages' next renders pull the refilled value. The real seam is just a transient, cosmetic divergence right after deploy, before any rebake or expiry reconciles the two shells; it's not a copy violation since the visible text never claims cross-page equality, just "bake #hex."

Initial state disagreement across build workers is expected and by design, but the cross-page runtime convergence claim really needs verification on preview, which is blocked by deployment protection for me — Eric would need to trigger the rebake press himself since it requires an authenticated POST. I should be upfront with him: local confirms the initial divergence is expected, but the convergence-after-rebake claim is only verified in theory pending his preview test. I also want to soften the overclaiming comment in shell/index-value.tsx.

I'll add one line noting that build workers bake independently, so shells can briefly disagree until the first revalidation converges them — observed 2026-08-20 on the lab build, which is solid evidence for §6. Then I'll make the edits: update the shell/index-value.tsx comment with that transient-divergence note, append it to design.md §6, commit as "docs+comment: record build-worker bake divergence", and push.

# The instrument design guide

`voice.md`'s sibling: that guide governs what a visitor reads, this one
governs what they see and press. It exists for the same reason — the design
drifts, and it drifts toward decoration. Every element on a demo earns its
place by answering one question: does this contribute to clarity? The page's
feel is a developer environment, not a course platform. Engineer, not
student.

The audience is four people at once — an aspiring developer, a non-technical
visitor, a junior, a senior — and they get **one experience legible at all
levels, never per-level modes**. When a value needs to reach all four, encode
it redundantly (two channels, one display), don't fork the interface.

---

## 1. The fixed grammar

Every demo sits in the same chassis, zones in fixed positions — like a car's
cockpit or an editor's panes, a visitor who has used one instrument has used
them all:

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ ● live                        SLOW MOTION ⭘ │  chrome: state left, view right
│                                              │
│  bake #64f93b                                │  the specimen
│  provenance rows · one narration caption     │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ [ actions, in execution order ]              │  the deck
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ ▸ bake.ts + actions.ts       docs ↗ source ↗ │  reference bar
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

- **Chrome, top-left — the state gauge.** `live` (cyan) at rest, `working`
  (amber) while any server round trip is out. One in-flight signal per
  instrument; this is it.
- **Chrome, top-right — view controls.** Mode switches (slow motion) live in
  the corner every editor keeps its view switches. Actions never live here.
  Empty when a demo has no alternate view.
- **Body — the specimen.** The observed value large, provenance rows as one
  aligned table, one narration caption. All describing text in one place.
- **Deck — actions only.** Execution order, left to right. When a flow has
  real sequence, the controls diagram it (numbered steps, an arrow, the later
  step dark until the earlier one fires). A deck may end in a **result chip —
  output, never input** — when the platform's own label for the sequence's
  outcome is knowable by rule (exhibit 02: `revalidated · tag-based
  deletion`, the badge Vercel files the refill under).
- **Reference bar — the status bar every editor ends in.** The code drawer's
  disclosure left (source opens inside the chassis, native `<details>`, zero
  JS); `docs` and `source` links pinned right, positioned so clicking them
  never toggles the drawer. Row height mirrors the chrome header.

What the grammar deliberately lacks: a panel label (the intro prose names the
subject once) and a readout footer (the source in the drawer is the spec
plate — a reader who wants identifiers is the reader who opens it).

Outside the chassis: exhibit order rides in the eyebrow (`02 · caching &
revalidation`) where engineers read identifiers — no watermark chapter
numerals. Asides are set as `/* code comments */` in comment-gray mono,
because that is what they are.

## 2. Feedback

Anything in flight says so three ways: the gauge flips to `working`, the
specimen dims and pulses, and when the new value lands it takes one amber
wash (`.ht-land` — key-remount, skips first paint, reduced-motion safe) and
settles. No silent updates, ever.

The React rule underneath: **client-owned state paints on the click frame;
only the server sync lives in a transition.** A mode flip inside the same
transition as its `router.refresh()` freezes the control until the round
trip resolves. While the flipped view waits for the server, the copy must
narrate the in-flight window honestly rather than claim a state the screen
doesn't show (see the settling readout in `rebake-copy.ts`).

## 3. Copy and demo co-evolve

A demo that gains a capability can obsolete prose that was accurate the day
it shipped — voice.md's three passes check a line against the panel *as it
is*, so re-run them whenever the panel changes. (Evidence: voice.md §6,
2026-08-19.)

## 4. Migration state — complete, 2026-08-20

All five exhibits are on the grammar; the legacy shapes (`LivePanel`
`label`/`readout`, standalone `CodeBlock`, `DemoSection`'s links row) are
deleted, not deprecated. Judgment calls worth keeping:

- **The specimen is not a control.** Exhibit 04's form and exhibit 01's
  click-me button stay in the body: a form wired to a Server Action is the
  lesson, and filing the subject under controls would misrepresent it. The
  deck holds instrument controls only (03's rerun, 05's title form — which
  drives the instrument rather than being it).
- **Unique readout facts became narration lines**; redundant readouts were
  cut without replacement (03, 04 — their facts live in the intro, the
  captions, or the source).
- **The gauge is wired where a client owns the panel** (02, 05). 03's
  in-flight signal is carried by the row skeletons and the rerun button's
  pending label instead — honest, but not the gauge; wire it if the stream
  panel ever gains a client owner. 01 and 04 have no client round trip to
  gauge (04's form works with JavaScript off, which is its point).

### The lab — site shape, 2026-08-20

The collection outgrew the landing page (half the syllabus is made of
routes — parallel/intercepted, not-found, params, view transitions — and
cannot run inside one page), so the playground has a book shape: a
contents page at `/lab`, one route segment per chapter at `/lab/<slug>`,
`/latest` redirecting to the newest chapter. One registry
(`apps/web/app/[locale]/lab/syllabus.ts`) drives every list — contents
rows, the landing roadmap, the contents bar, page-turns, sitemap, OG
titles — so shipping a chapter is one entry flip: planned → next →
shipped, belief and navLabel added.

- **Chapter pages** render the same demo wrapper the landing shows, with
  the belief promoted to the page's h1 (the eyebrow demotes to a
  non-heading element). The frame adds the making-of aside (the folder's
  commit history + the checkpoints repo) and the page-turn row
  (prev · contents · next), and `/api/og` draws each chapter's card from
  its belief.
- **Index readings.** A chapter may put one true value from its running
  instrument on its contents row, each inside its own Suspense — the
  index is itself a partial-prerender demonstration. Truth rule: a
  per-visitor value says so ("your presses · 3"); a global-sounding
  count would be the index's first lie.
- **Vocabulary.** Visitor prose says *the lab* and *chapter* (voice.md
  §6, 2026-08-20). "Exhibit" remains the working word in code comments
  and these docs.

## 5. Banked

- The bake fingerprint is six hex characters — literally a CSS color — and
  the unlabeled `BakeSwatch` beside it renders that value. The discovery is
  intentional; the digest write-up is where it gets spelled out.
- Fruit/emoji hash encoding: rejected as primary (breaks instrument
  discipline), held as a possible easter-egg layer.
- Swatches in the machinery comparison rows: blocked until the string-based
  width-reservation (`StableSlot`) grows a JSX-safe design.
- Digest beats banked: the side-effect-runs-twice warning; the
  swatch-is-the-hash reveal.
- Contents-row hover-prefetch readout: the lab's index rows already
  prefetch on hover via next/link — chapter 06 (navigation &
  prefetching) should claim that readout as its instrument in the site's
  own chrome.

## 6. Verification

`next dev` lies about cache semantics (`updateTag` entries survive reloads
that die on Vercel) — preview deploys are the truth-bench for anything
touching `use cache`.

The verified badge sequence for the rebake flow on Vercel (2026-08-20,
preview logs): `PRERENDER` on first visit → `HIT` → `BYPASS` for the action
POST → `REVALIDATED`, reason "Tag-based deletion", for the request that
refills. `updateTag` never produces `STALE` (that badge is
stale-while-revalidate: `revalidateTag` or a lapsed `cacheLife` window), and
the tag-deletion miss is labeled `REVALIDATED`, not `MISS`. Copy that names
log badges must match this. The React DevTools extension throws spurious "The
children should not have changed if we pass in the same set." errors on
transition commits here; stacks resolving to `chrome-extension://…` are the
extension's mirror desyncing, not an app bug.

## 7. Keeping this current

Same contract as voice.md §9: update on a decision that no rule here
predicted, never on a schedule. §1–§3 are the rules and should grow
reluctantly; §4–§6 are state and evidence — keep them dated, and correct
them when the code moves.

Eric's issue is that navigating between pages shows a visible scroll-to-top animation instead of instantly loading at the top. I suspect this is caused by `scroll-behavior: smooth` on the html element interfering with Next.js's router scroll reset, turning what should be an instant jump into an animated scroll.

Since this is a debugging question, I should invoke the systematic-debugging skill before proposing any fix, and verify my hypothesis empirically rather than just theorizing. I recall Next.js has logic to temporarily force `scroll-behavior: auto` during navigation to avoid exactly this conflict, so I need to check whether that's actually working as expected here.

Now I recall the specific fix: Next.js changed `handleSmoothScroll` to only force `scroll-behavior: auto` when the `<html>` element has a `data-scroll-behavior="smooth"` attribute, avoiding a forced reflow. This means if your CSS sets smooth scrolling globally but you don't add that data attribute to `<html>`, navigations will animate to the top instead of jumping instantly — the fix is adding `data-scroll-behavior="smooth"` to the html tag.

# Systematic Debugging

## Overview

**Core principle:** ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure.

**Violating the letter of this process is violating the spirit of debugging.**

## The Iron Law

```
NO FIXES WITHOUT ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION FIRST
```

If you haven't completed Phase 1, you cannot propose fixes.

## When to Use

Use for ANY technical issue:
- Test failures
- Bugs in production
- Unexpected behavior
- Performance problems
- Build failures
- Integration issues

**Use this ESPECIALLY when:**
- Under time pressure (emergencies make guessing tempting)
- "Just one quick fix" seems obvious
- You've already tried multiple fixes
- Previous fix didn't work
- You don't fully understand the issue

**Don't skip when:**
- Issue seems simple (simple bugs have root causes too)
- You're in a hurry (rushing guarantees rework)
- Manager wants it fixed NOW (systematic is faster than thrashing)

## The Four Phases

You MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.

### Phase 1: Root Cause Investigation

**BEFORE attempting ANY fix:**

1. **Read Error Messages Carefully**
   - Don't skip past errors or warnings
   - They often contain the exact solution
   - Read stack traces completely
   - Note line numbers, file paths, error codes

2. **Reproduce Consistently**
   - Can you trigger it reliably?
   - What are the exact steps?
   - Does it happen every time?
   - If not reproducible → gather more data, don't guess

3. **Check Recent Changes**
   - What changed that could cause this?
   - Git diff, recent commits
   - New dependencies, config changes
   - Environmental differences

4. **Gather Evidence in Multi-Component Systems**

   **WHEN system has multiple components (CI → build → signing, API → service → database):**

   **BEFORE proposing fixes, add diagnostic instrumentation:**
   ```
   For EACH component boundary:
     - Log what data enters component
     - Log what data exits component
     - Verify environment/config propagation
     - Check state at each layer

   Run once to gather evidence showing WHERE it breaks
   THEN analyze evidence to identify failing component
   THEN investigate that specific component
   ```

   **Example (multi-layer system):**
   ```bash
   # Layer 1: Workflow
   echo "=== Secrets available in workflow: ==="
   echo "IDENTITY: ${IDENTITY:+SET}${IDENTITY:-UNSET}"

   # Layer 2: Build script
   echo "=== Env vars in build script: ==="
   env | grep IDENTITY || echo "IDENTITY not in environment"

   # Layer 3: Signing script
   echo "=== Keychain state: ==="
   security list-keychains
   security find-identity -v

   # Layer 4: Actual signing
   codesign --sign "$IDENTITY" --verbose=4 "$APP"
   ```

   **This reveals:** Which layer fails (secrets → workflow ✓, workflow → build ✗)

5. **Trace Data Flow**

   **WHEN error is deep in call stack:**

   See `root-cause-tracing.md` in this directory for the complete backward tracing technique.

   **Quick version:**
   - Where does bad value originate?
   - What called this with bad value?
   - Keep tracing up until you find the source
   - Fix at source, not at symptom

### Phase 2: Pattern Analysis

**Find the pattern before fixing:**

1. **Find Working Examples**
   - Locate similar working code in same codebase
   - What works that's similar to what's broken?

2. **Compare Against References**
   - If implementing pattern, read reference implementation COMPLETELY
   - Don't skim - read every line
   - Understand the pattern fully before applying

3. **Identify Differences**
   - What's different between working and broken?
   - List every difference, however small
   - Don't assume "that can't matter"

4. **Understand Dependencies**
   - What other components does this need?
   - What settings, config, environment?
   - What assumptions does it make?

### Phase 3: Hypothesis and Testing

**Scientific method:**

1. **Form Single Hypothesis**
   - State clearly: "I think X is the root cause because Y"
   - Write it down
   - Be specific, not vague

2. **Test Minimally**
   - Make the SMALLEST possible change to test hypothesis
   - One variable at a time
   - Don't fix multiple things at once

3. **Verify Before Continuing**
   - Did it work? Yes → Phase 4
   - Didn't work? Form NEW hypothesis
   - DON'T add more fixes on top

4. **When You Don't Know**
   - Say "I don't understand X"
   - Don't pretend to know
   - Ask for help
   - Research more

### Phase 4: Implementation

**Fix the root cause, not the symptom:**

1. **Create Failing Test Case**
   - Simplest possible reproduction
   - Automated test if possible
   - One-off test script if no framework
   - MUST have before fixing
   - Use the `superpowers:test-driven-development` skill for writing proper failing tests

2. **Implement Single Fix**
   - Address the root cause identified
   - ONE change at a time
   - No "while I'm here" improvements
   - No bundled refactoring

3. **Verify Fix**
   - Test passes now?
   - No other tests broken?
   - Issue actually resolved?
   - Use the `superpowers:verification-before-completion` skill before claiming success

4. **If Fix Doesn't Work**
   - STOP
   - Count: How many fixes have you tried?
   - If < 3: Return to Phase 1, re-analyze with new information
   - **If ≥ 3: STOP and question the architecture (step 5 below)**
   - DON'T attempt Fix #4 without architectural discussion

5. **If 3+ Fixes Failed: Question Architecture**

   **Pattern indicating architectural problem:**
   - Each fix reveals new shared state/coupling/problem in different place
   - Fixes require "massive refactoring" to implement
   - Each fix creates new symptoms elsewhere

   **STOP and question fundamentals:**
   - Is this pattern fundamentally sound?
   - Are we "sticking with it through sheer inertia"?
   - Should we refactor architecture vs. continue fixing symptoms?

   **Discuss with your human partner before attempting more fixes**

   This is NOT a failed hypothesis - this is a wrong architecture.

## Red Flags - STOP and Follow Process

If you catch yourself thinking:
- "Quick fix for now, investigate later"
- "Just try changing X and see if it works"
- "Add multiple changes, run tests"
- "Skip the test, I'll manually verify"
- "It's probably X, let me fix that"
- "I don't fully understand but this might work"
- "Pattern says X but I'll adapt it differently"
- "Here are the main problems: [lists fixes without investigation]"
- Proposing solutions before tracing data flow
- **"One more fix attempt" (when already tried 2+)**
- **Each fix reveals new problem in different place**

**ALL of these mean: STOP. Return to Phase 1.**

**If 3+ fixes failed:** Question the architecture (see Phase 4.5)

## your human partner's Signals You're Doing It Wrong

**Watch for these redirections:**
- "Is that not happening?" - You assumed without verifying
- "Will it show us...?" - You should have added evidence gathering
- "Stop guessing" - You're proposing fixes without understanding
- "Ultra-think this" - Question fundamentals, not just symptoms
- "We're stuck?" (frustrated) - Your approach isn't working

**When you see these:** STOP. Return to Phase 1.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Issue is simple, don't need process" | Simple issues have root causes too. Process is fast for simple bugs. |
| "Emergency, no time for process" | Systematic debugging is FASTER than guess-and-check thrashing. |
| "Just try this first, then investigate" | First fix sets the pattern. Do it right from the start. |
| "I'll write test after confirming fix works" | Untested fixes don't stick. Test first proves it. |
| "Multiple fixes at once saves time" | Can't isolate what worked. Causes new bugs. |
| "Reference too long, I'll adapt the pattern" | Partial understanding guarantees bugs. Read it completely. |
| "I see the problem, let me fix it" | Seeing symptoms ≠ understanding root cause. |
| "One more fix attempt" (after 2+ failures) | 3+ failures = architectural problem. Question pattern, don't fix again. |

## Quick Reference

| Phase | Key Activities | Success Criteria |
|-------|---------------|------------------|
| **1. Root Cause** | Read errors, reproduce, check changes, gather evidence | Understand WHAT and WHY |
| **2. Pattern** | Find working examples, compare | Identify differences |
| **3. Hypothesis** | Form theory, test minimally | Confirmed or new hypothesis |
| **4. Implementation** | Create test, fix, verify | Bug resolved, tests pass |

## When Process Reveals "No Root Cause"

If systematic investigation reveals issue is truly environmental, timing-dependent, or external:

1. You've completed the process
2. Document what you investigated
3. Implement appropriate handling (retry, timeout, error message)
4. Add monitoring/logging for future investigation

**But:** 95% of "no root cause" cases are incomplete investigation.

## Supporting Techniques

These techniques are part of systematic debugging and available in this directory:

- **`root-cause-tracing.md`** - Trace bugs backward through call stack to find original trigger
- **`defense-in-depth.md`** - Add validation at multiple layers after finding root cause
- **`condition-based-waiting.md`** - Replace arbitrary timeouts with condition polling

content.text:
**Root cause found, verified, and fixed** (you clarified mid-investigation that both behaviors should hold, so I applied the one-line fix rather than stopping at the diagnosis).

**The root cause is a missing attribute, not the smooth scroll itself.** Two halves that don't know about each other:

1. `apps/web/app/layout.tsx` puts Tailwind's `scroll-smooth` (`scroll-behavior: smooth`) on `<html>` — there since the very first landing-page commit, for the contents-bar anchors and the seats CTA.
2. Next 16's router wraps every navigation's scroll-to-top in `disableSmoothScrollDuringRouteTransition` (read directly from the installed 16.3.1 source). That function only suppresses smooth scrolling **if `<html>` carries `data-scroll-behavior="smooth"`** — it deliberately refuses to call `getComputedStyle` to detect the CSS, because that forces a layout pass on every navigation. No attribute → it returns early, and the router's `scrollTo(0, …)` runs with your smooth CSS still active, so the new page animates up from wherever you were. There's a one-time warning about exactly this, but only in dev; production is silent.

Why you never saw it before this branch: the landing page had no page-to-page navigations, only hash scrolls — and hash scrolls are explicitly exempt from the suppression (`onlyHashChange`). The lab added the site's first real router links, which is why it surfaced now.

**Evidence** (production build, Playwright, sampling `window.scrollY` after clicking a chapter link from a scrolled position):

- As shipped: 1443 → 1399 → 1276 → 961 → … → 0 over ~900ms — the animated glide you saw.
- Same session, same navigation, with *only* `document.documentElement.dataset.scrollBehavior = "smooth"` set: **y = 0 at the first sample, 61ms in.** One variable, flipped result.
- Anchor click with the attribute in place: still eases 17 → 725 → 2019 → 2994 — the glide survives, because hash scrolls bypass the suppression.

**The fix:** `data-scroll-behavior="smooth"` added to the `<html>` element in `layout.tsx`, with a comment stating the constraint. Re-verified end-to-end on a rebuilt production server: route navigation from y=1443 opens at the top by the first 68ms sample; the landing's `#demo-03` anchor still animates. Biome, tsc, and all 209 tests green. Pushed as `5e08812d` on the PR #392 branch, and the gotcha is recorded in my env-quirks memory so it doesn't get rediscovered the hard way.

# The instrument design guide

`voice.md`'s sibling: that guide governs what a visitor reads, this one
governs what they see and press. It exists for the same reason — the design
drifts, and it drifts toward decoration. Every element on a demo earns its
place by answering one question: does this contribute to clarity? The page's
feel is a developer environment, not a course platform. Engineer, not
student.

The audience is four people at once — an aspiring developer, a non-technical
visitor, a junior, a senior — and they get **one experience legible at all
levels, never per-level modes**. When a value needs to reach all four, encode
it redundantly (two channels, one display), don't fork the interface.

---

## 1. The fixed grammar

Every demo sits in the same chassis, zones in fixed positions — like a car's
cockpit or an editor's panes, a visitor who has used one instrument has used
them all:

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ ● live                        SLOW MOTION ⭘ │  chrome: state left, view right
│                                              │
│  bake #64f93b                                │  the specimen
│  provenance rows · one narration caption     │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ [ actions, in execution order ]              │  the deck
├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ ▸ bake.ts + actions.ts       docs ↗ source ↗ │  reference bar
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

- **Chrome, top-left — the state gauge.** `live` (cyan) at rest, `working`
  (amber) while any server round trip is out. One in-flight signal per
  instrument; this is it.
- **Chrome, top-right — view controls.** Mode switches (slow motion) live in
  the corner every editor keeps its view switches. Actions never live here.
  Empty when a demo has no alternate view.
- **Body — the specimen.** The observed value large, provenance rows as one
  aligned table, one narration caption. All describing text in one place.
- **Deck — actions only.** Execution order, left to right. When a flow has
  real sequence, the controls diagram it (numbered steps, an arrow, the later
  step dark until the earlier one fires). A deck may end in a **result chip —
  output, never input** — when the platform's own label for the sequence's
  outcome is knowable by rule (exhibit 02: `revalidated · tag-based
  deletion`, the badge Vercel files the refill under).
- **Reference bar — the status bar every editor ends in.** The code drawer's
  disclosure left (source opens inside the chassis, native `<details>`, zero
  JS); `docs` and `source` links pinned right, positioned so clicking them
  never toggles the drawer. Row height mirrors the chrome header.

What the grammar deliberately lacks: a panel label (the intro prose names the
subject once) and a readout footer (the source in the drawer is the spec
plate — a reader who wants identifiers is the reader who opens it).

Outside the chassis: exhibit order rides in the eyebrow (`02 · caching &
revalidation`) where engineers read identifiers — no watermark chapter
numerals. Asides are set as `/* code comments */` in comment-gray mono,
because that is what they are.

## 2. Feedback

Anything in flight says so three ways: the gauge flips to `working`, the
specimen dims and pulses, and when the new value lands it takes one amber
wash (`.ht-land` — key-remount, skips first paint, reduced-motion safe) and
settles. No silent updates, ever.

The React rule underneath: **client-owned state paints on the click frame;
only the server sync lives in a transition.** A mode flip inside the same
transition as its `router.refresh()` freezes the control until the round
trip resolves. While the flipped view waits for the server, the copy must
narrate the in-flight window honestly rather than claim a state the screen
doesn't show (see the settling readout in `rebake-copy.ts`).

## 3. Copy and demo co-evolve

A demo that gains a capability can obsolete prose that was accurate the day
it shipped — voice.md's three passes check a line against the panel *as it
is*, so re-run them whenever the panel changes. (Evidence: voice.md §6,
2026-08-19.)

## 4. Migration state — complete, 2026-08-20

All five exhibits are on the grammar; the legacy shapes (`LivePanel`
`label`/`readout`, standalone `CodeBlock`, `DemoSection`'s links row) are
deleted, not deprecated. Judgment calls worth keeping:

- **The specimen is not a control.** Exhibit 04's form and exhibit 01's
  click-me button stay in the body: a form wired to a Server Action is the
  lesson, and filing the subject under controls would misrepresent it. The
  deck holds instrument controls only (03's rerun, 05's title form — which
  drives the instrument rather than being it).
- **Unique readout facts became narration lines**; redundant readouts were
  cut without replacement (03, 04 — their facts live in the intro, the
  captions, or the source).
- **The gauge is wired where a client owns the panel** (02, 05). 03's
  in-flight signal is carried by the row skeletons and the rerun button's
  pending label instead — honest, but not the gauge; wire it if the stream
  panel ever gains a client owner. 01 and 04 have no client round trip to
  gauge (04's form works with JavaScript off, which is its point).

### The lab — site shape, 2026-08-20

The collection outgrew the landing page (half the syllabus is made of
routes — parallel/intercepted, not-found, params, view transitions — and
cannot run inside one page), so the playground has a book shape: a
contents page at `/lab`, one route segment per chapter at `/lab/<slug>`,
`/latest` redirecting to the newest chapter. One registry
(`apps/web/app/[locale]/lab/syllabus.ts`) drives every list — contents
rows, the landing roadmap, the contents bar, page-turns, sitemap, OG

shipped, belief and navLabel added.

  the belief promoted to the page's h1 (the eyebrow demotes to a

  instrument on its contents row, each inside its own Suspense — the
  index is itself a partial-prerender demonstration. Truth rule: a
  per-visitor value says so ("your presses · 3"); a global-sounding
  count would be the index's first lie.

the tag-deletion miss is labeled `REVALIDATED`, not `MISS`. Copy that names

children should not have changed if we pass in the same set." errors on
transition commits here; stacks resolving to `chrome-extension://…` are the
extension's mirror desyncing, not an app bug.

content:
Fair point. I nearly forgot about the learn path. Indeed we do need a separate way of organizing the learning path. The demos are live, running references, a destination of sorts, while the learning path is about how to get there when you're a beginner, junior, or senior crossing over to Next.js. It's an open discussion now whether this path should be scoped to cohorts only or be public. I'm leaning public. We might want to expand into more complex territory like multi-tenant applications and how things work under these constraints; that would open up learning paths not scoped to just the feature but the feature within a constrainted environment. The demos should be their own abstraction layer. Learning paths have more of a narrative structure, too. They're educating with a certain goal in mind while the demo is a truthful interaction with the mechanism. It wants to disabuse you of any misconceptions, yes, but that's an inherent property of all things people have to make an effort to really understand.

I guess the real question is, what does the cohort use then? And I think the answer to that is clear now, too. The cohort is a structured experience that relies on existing demos and learning paths, and which features either recorded video content or live streams. The cohort is the place where we would teach comprehensive web development from the ground up, depending on which cohort we run.

content.text:
The model you just articulated is sound, and I'd argue it's not just organization — it resolves a tension that's been sitting in the design docs since the beginning. Let me sharpen its edges and name what falls out of it.

**The boundary between lab and paths is one rule: the lab doesn't know who's reading; a path knows exactly who's reading.** That's the whole abstraction. And it retroactively explains design.md's four-audience rule — "one experience legible at all levels, never per-level modes" was never really a ban on levels, it was levels not having a home. Now they have one. The lab stays audience-agnostic so a chapter can be dropped into a code review without carrying curriculum; a path is *made of* audience — "junior," "senior crossing over from React SPA-land" is its first design input. Your line about misconceptions fits the same split: in the lab, the misconception is the door (the belief is the H1); on a path, misconceptions are potholes you hit en route to somewhere else. Same confrontation, different structural position — which is why paths won't dilute the lab's identity even though they'll also disabuse.

**One consequence worth adopting as law when paths get built:** paths cite chapters for every mechanism claim, and never restate mechanism in their own prose. Tutorials rot — that's the known disease of narrative technical content. But if mechanism-truth lives only in the lab (which the weekly cadence keeps current) and paths carry only narrative and sequencing, then path-rot is narrative-rot only, and voice.md §7's time-hardening stays compositional instead of needing to be re-fought in every path. This is the practical payoff of "the demos should be their own abstraction layer."

**On public vs. cohort-gated: your lean is right, and your own FAQ already committed to it.** "The playground doesn't get better if you buy the cohort" is a stance about what's for sale — and what the cohort sells, by your own definition just now, is structure, cadence, feedback, and people, not content. Gating paths would starve the funnel to protect an asset the cohort's value doesn't rest on. The economics compound in your favor too: if paths are public, every hour of cohort prep that isn't live teaching accretes into a permanent public asset instead of evaporating after the session. The honest trade-off is maintenance surface — public paths are a promise to keep them current — but the citation rule above is precisely what makes that promise cheap.

**The constraint-paths idea is the most interesting expansion**, and I'd name what it really is: the lab proves mechanisms *in isolation*; real applications are mechanisms *composing under constraints*. So paths come in two species — audience-shaped (who you are) and constraint-shaped (where you're building: multi-tenant, EU-data, cost-bounded). And there's a gift waiting in the repo: hasToggle *is* a multi-tenant SaaS template — better-auth organizations, active org as tenant id. A multi-tenant path could keep the site's core property of teaching from the running artifact rather than from hypotheticals. The self-demonstration doctrine extends up a layer.

**On "what does the cohort use" — your answer, stated structurally:** lab chapters are landmarks, paths are routes through them, and a cohort is a *scheduled, guided traversal* of a route — same map, walked together, with a coach and a camera. Two things in the repo already prefigure this. The masterclass is literally a cohort-layer specimen: dated URL, presenter-driven, beat-gated. And its beat transport — the stepper/beats machinery you built in July — is a natural candidate for the path layer's sequencing primitive, so paths may cost less to build than they appear. Which also sorts the attic: `/learn` today holds proto-specimens of every layer mixed together — ref-vs-state and qa-stories are path-lessons, the masterclass is a cohort artifact, Hazel is a parked lesson. The model you just described is the filing system they've been waiting for.

Nothing shipped this week needs rework — the lab's abstraction is exactly the one this model requires, and Hazel's banked note already points at the path layer.

**Still genuinely open, for whenever you want a design round on it:** the formal public/gated call (your lean, said out loud, would settle it); the path unit's shape (single lesson pages vs. beat-sequenced multi-step routes — I suspect the latter, given the transport exists); whether constraint-paths narrate the template repo or eventually want a running companion app; and whether paths get their own registry the way the lab did. When you call the layer model settled, it belongs in the repo per your rule — my suggestion would be a short site-architecture note beside voice.md and design.md rather than stretching design.md further, since it now governs three surfaces, not one. I've noted the model and your public lean in memory either way.
